content.p: Laci Peterson was 27 and about eight months pregnant when she was reported missing from her home in Modesto, California, on Christmas Eve 2002. Four months later the bodies of Laci and of the son the couple had planned to name Conner washed ashore on the edge of San Francisco Bay. Her husband, Scott Peterson, was convicted in 2004 of murdering both: first degree for Laci, second degree for their unborn son. He was sentenced to death, but the California Supreme Court threw out the death sentence in 2020 while leaving the convictions in place, and in December 2021 a judge ordered him to serve life with no chance of parole.

Peterson has always said he is innocent. Since 2024 the Los Angeles Innocence Project has pressed his case, and in April or May 2026 a San Mateo County judge rejected its latest petition. The prosecutors who handled the case say the verdict has held for two decades.

Peterson told police that everything had seemed fine when he left the house on 24 December. He had told a neighbour he was going golfing, prosecutors later said, but he drove to the Berkeley Marina, almost 90 miles away, and said he went fishing in a small aluminium boat. NBC Bay Area noted it was a boat he had recently bought and that his family had not known he owned. Laci was reported missing that day, and a large search began.

A month later the case changed direction. Amber Frey, a massage therapist living in Fresno, told reporters that she and Peterson had been in a romantic relationship, and that he had told her he was not married. She had contacted police on 30 December. Prosecutors said Peterson told Frey he had "lost" his wife and would be spending his first Christmas alone, a conversation that took place while Laci was still alive. In March 2003 police began treating the disappearance as a homicide.

In mid-April 2003 the remains of an infant and, a day later, of an adult woman were found on the shore at Richmond's Point Isabel, a mile apart and a few miles from the spot where Peterson said he had been fishing. Police identified them as Conner and Laci. The same day, Peterson was arrested near San Diego. His hair and goatee were bleached, and police said he had about $15,000 in cash, his brother's identity card and several mobile phones on him. He pleaded not guilty to two charges of murder and hired the celebrity lawyer Mark Geragos.

Publicity was so heavy that a Stanislaus County judge ruled Peterson could not get a fair trial in his hometown, and the case was moved about 90 miles to Redwood City in San Mateo County. It ran for roughly five to six months, depending on the account. There was no crime scene and no murder weapon, and the case rested on circumstantial evidence. Prosecutors argued that Peterson wanted a life free of marriage and a child. Frey testified that he had told her he was a widower and had lied about where he lived, and jurors heard recordings of their calls made after she agreed to cooperate with police.

The jury changed during the proceedings. Two jurors were removed for misconduct and a third left after arguments in the jury room. One of the replacements, Richelle Nice, later became central to the appeals.

On 12 November 2004 the jury found Peterson guilty of first-degree murder over Laci and second-degree murder over Conner. It then unanimously recommended death. Oxygen dates that recommendation and the judge's sentence to 13 December 2004; CNN and Fox 11 say he was formally sentenced to death in 2005, Fox 11 giving March. He was sent to San Quentin.

On 24 August 2020 the California Supreme Court upheld his convictions and overturned the death sentence, in a unanimous decision. "We reject Peterson's claim that he received an unfair trial as to guilt and thus affirm his convictions for murder," the justices wrote. But they found that the trial judge "made a series of clear and significant errors in jury selection" and that those errors damaged his right to an impartial jury when the jury weighed punishment. Many prospective jurors had been dismissed over questionnaire answers opposing the death penalty, even though they said they could follow the law.

Prosecutors were free to seek death again. Stanislaus County District Attorney Birgit Fladager said in 2021 that she would not, after consulting Laci's family, who said the "process is simply too painful to endure once again."

On 8 December 2021 Judge Anne-Christine Massullo resentenced Peterson, then 49, to life without parole for Laci's murder and a concurrent term of 15 years to life for Conner's. Laci's mother, Sharon Rocha, told him in court: "Laci and Conner will always be dead, and you will always be their murderer." Peterson was moved from San Quentin to Mule Creek State Prison in 2022.

Two months after it overturned the death sentence, in October 2020, the state's high court sent the convictions back to a lower court because of Juror No. 7, Nice, who had not disclosed that she had sought a restraining order while pregnant. Peterson's lawyers said her answers on the questionnaire were false and that she had committed misconduct.

After hearings in which Nice testified, Judge Massullo ruled on 20 December 2022 that Nice had given false answers but that this did not require a new trial. She found that Nice's responses "were not motivated by pre-existing or improper bias" and came instead from "a combination of good faith misunderstanding of the questions and sloppiness in answering." Nice had sworn she did not mention the restraining order because "it never crossed my mind, ever." ABC7 San Francisco reported in 2026 that the Los Angeles Innocence Project is challenging that ruling in the California Supreme Court, and KFI and KRON each described a juror-misconduct petition as still pending there.

The Los Angeles Innocence Project, a nonprofit that works with Cal State LA, announced in January 2024 that it represented Peterson and was investigating his claim of actual innocence. It then appeared before Judge Elizabeth Hill in Redwood City and asked for DNA testing, including of stains on a mattress found in a burned-out van about a mile from the Petersons' home the day after Laci vanished, and of evidence from a burglary across the street from their house. The defence theory was that Laci might have encountered the burglars.

On 29 May 2024 Hill granted testing of only one of 14 items: roughly 15 inches of duct tape found on Laci's pants. She said she was ruling on evidence, not on whether Peterson should have a new trial. Prosecutors argued the case was settled. "We were right then and we are right now," said Dave Harris of the Stanislaus County District Attorney's office. A judge also allowed the defence to review some discovery material from the 2004 case, such as police interview transcripts.

In April 2025 the project filed a proposed petition of nearly 400 pages with the California Court of Appeal in San Francisco, accompanied by a 126-page declaration from Peterson. It argued that new scientific evidence put the date of Conner's death later than at trial, that a water-movement expert could show Laci's body was not dumped where police said, and that jurors never heard about the burglary and the burned van. It also alleged confirmation bias and possible Brady violations, meaning failures to disclose evidence, by Modesto police and the district attorney's office; it said police had destroyed potentially critical evidence. Prosecutors have said the burglary had nothing to do with the case. A Stanislaus deputy district attorney said he believed the court had rejected that first filing because of a technical violation.

ABC7 and KRON report that a habeas corpus petition was then filed in August 2025. They say the project argued Peterson was convicted on false scientific evidence, and KRON adds that its investigators had carried out more than 50 witness interviews.

The news reports date Judge Hill's decision differently. ABC7 and KRON reported on 29 April 2026 that she had declined to review the new evidence and denied the petition as procedurally barred or lacking merit. KFI AM 640 reported on 14 May that she had rejected all 14 claims in a 116-page ruling, finding them "procedurally barred, meritless, or both" and nothing "new, admissible, nor material." Oxygen also places the denial of all 14 claims in May 2026.

Deputy director Hannah Brown said the project was "disappointed by the court's ruling on every level" and that it showed "a profound misunderstanding and misapplication of the law applied to habeas corpus petitions." District Attorney Jeff Laugero called the claims "recycled, repackaged and rebranded arguments" and said that "no credible 'new evidence' was presented." The project said it would take the petition to a higher court. As of July 2026, the latest reports describe the appeal as planned, not decided.

Peterson, now 53, is held at Mule Creek State Prison. A&E scheduled a documentary, "Scott Peterson: The New Evidence," to examine the Innocence Project's claims. Al Brocchini, a former Modesto police detective, has dismissed the burglary theory, arguing that the two men linked to the robbery had alibis, and said in a 2024 documentary that "the jury got it right."
